Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally in the first weeks and months after birth.  

Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. The EPDS is just 10 questions about the past seven days; there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. When we’re done I’ll add up the scores and we can talk about what they mean and what support might help.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, I can still laugh, but it feels a little forced. Maybe once or twice in the past week I’ve smiled at something my partner said, but it doesn’t come as easily as before the baby. So—yes, sometimes, but definitely not as much as I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes—like when my husband made that silly joke about diaper explosions I did chuckle—but mostly I have to remind myself to lighten up. It doesn’t come naturally right now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I still get excited about little things—like our afternoon walk to the park yesterday—but the spark isn’t as strong. I look forward to them, yet once they happen I feel kind of “meh.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was fussy for almost an hour and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or that I wasn’t soothing her the “right” way. I know, rationally, babies just cry, but the thought still pops in: “What if it’s my fault?”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly worry her breathing sounds different, even though she’s perfectly fine. The worry comes out of nowhere, but it passes pretty quickly once I take a breath or my partner reassures me.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just a quick rush of “what-if.” It’s gone in seconds, and I can settle myself.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like this morning—she wouldn’t settle after her 3 a.m. feed, and I still had to fold laundry and answer a text from my mom. For a minute it felt like everything was piling up, but I took a breath, put her in the sling, and chipped away at it. I manage, it’s just… heavier than it used to be.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I’ve had trouble drifting off a couple of nights, but it’s more my mind racing about tomorrow’s to-do list than feeling unhappy. Once I’m asleep I stay asleep—unless she wakes me, of course.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I do feel that way some of the time. Not all day, but there are moments—especially in the late afternoon—when I just feel kind of down and empty. It usually lifts if I get out of the house or talk to a friend, but the sad feeling keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—like two evenings ago when she wouldn’t latch and I felt stuck on the couch. It wasn’t an all-day thing, just sudden tears that stopped once my partner handed me a glass of water and told me to breathe.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I might feel overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (partner present, no report of self-harm ideation)

Key symptoms endorsed  
- Intermittent low mood, “empty” spells, worse late afternoon  
- Reduced enjoyment/“meh” reaction to previously pleasant activities  
- Episodic tearfulness (twice this week) linked to infant-feeding stress  
- Unwarranted self-blame when baby fussy; ruminative “what-if” worries about infant safety  
- Transient, situational anxiety (seconds-long “rush”); no full panic attacks  
- Periodic sense of being overwhelmed; copes with planning/support but describes tasks as “heavier”  
- Occasional sleep-onset difficulty related to racing thoughts, not mood per se; no middle-insomnia unrelated to infant feeds  

Patterns / risk indicators  
- Affective: recurrent sadness, anhedonia, crying spells  
- Cognitive: guilty attributions, worry without precipitant  
- Functional: coping intact but effortful; no impairment in basic self-/baby-care  
- Safety: Denies thoughts of self-harm; protective factor = partner support  

Screening impression  
Moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms above “baby blues” threshold; not meeting crisis level. Continue monitoring, consider standardized follow-up (EPDS) and psychoeducation; refer for formal evaluation if symptoms persist >2 weeks or worsen.
